{{Short description|Mathematical operation on matrices}}
{{CS1 config|mode=cs1}}
{{for|the Kronecker product of representations of symmetric groups |Kronecker coefficient}}
In [[mathematics]], the '''Kronecker product''', sometimes denoted by &otimes;, is an [[operation (mathematics)|operation]] on two [[matrix (mathematics)|matrices]] of arbitrary size resulting in a [[block matrix]]. It is a specialization of the [[tensor product]] (which is denoted by the same symbol) from vectors to matrices and gives the matrix of the [[tensor product]] linear map with respect to a standard choice of [[Basis (linear algebra)|basis]]. The Kronecker product is to be distinguished from the usual [[matrix multiplication]], which is an entirely different operation. The Kronecker product is also sometimes called '''matrix direct product'''.<ref>
{{cite web
 |last=Weisstein  |first=Eric W.
 |title=Kronecker product
 |website=mathworld.wolfram.com  |language=en
 |url=https://mathworld.wolfram.com/KroneckerProduct.html
 |access-date=2020-09-06
}}
</ref>

The Kronecker product is named after the German mathematician [[Leopold Kronecker]] (1823–1891), even though there is little evidence that he was the first to define and use it. The Kronecker product has also been called the ''Zehfuss matrix'', and the ''Zehfuss product'', after {{ill|Johann Georg Zehfuss|de|Georg Zehfuss}}, who in 1858 described this matrix operation, but ''Kronecker product'' is currently the most widely used term.<ref>
{{cite journal
| first = G.  | last = Zehfuss
| year = 1858
| title = Ueber eine gewisse Determinante
| journal = Zeitschrift für Mathematik und Physik
| volume = 3  | pages = 298–301
| url = http://resolver.sub.uni-goettingen.de/purl?PPN599415665_0003
}}
</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Henderson|first1=Harold V.|last2=Pukelsheim|first2=Friedrich|last3=Searle|first3=Shayle R.|date=1983|title=On the history of the kronecker product|journal=Linear and Multilinear Algebra|volume=14|issue=2|pages=113–120|doi=10.1080/03081088308817548|issn=0308-1087|hdl=1813/32834|hdl-access=free}}</ref> The misattribution to Kronecker rather than Zehfuss was due to [[Kurt Hensel]].<ref>{{Cite book |last=Sayed |first=Ali H. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=VNWbEAAAQBAJ&dq=maximum+norm&pg=PA41 |title=Inference and Learning from Data: Foundations |date=2022-12-22 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |isbn=978-1-009-21812-2 |language=en}}</ref>

== Definition ==
If '''A''' is an {{nowrap|''m'' × ''n''}} matrix and '''B''' is a {{nowrap|''p'' × ''q''}} matrix, then the Kronecker product {{nowrap|'''A''' &otimes; '''B'''}} is the {{nowrap|''pm'' × ''qn''}} block matrix:

: <math>\mathbf{A}\otimes\mathbf{B} = \begin{bmatrix}
  a_{11} \mathbf{B} & \cdots & a_{1n}\mathbf{B} \\
             \vdots & \ddots &           \vdots \\
  a_{m1} \mathbf{B} & \cdots & a_{mn} \mathbf{B}
\end{bmatrix}, </math>

more explicitly:

: <math>{\mathbf{A}\otimes\mathbf{B}} = \begin{bmatrix}
   a_{11} b_{11} & a_{11} b_{12} & \cdots & a_{11} b_{1q} &
                   \cdots & \cdots & a_{1n} b_{11} & a_{1n} b_{12} & \cdots & a_{1n} b_{1q} \\
   a_{11} b_{21} & a_{11} b_{22} & \cdots & a_{11} b_{2q} &
                   \cdots & \cdots & a_{1n} b_{21} & a_{1n} b_{22} & \cdots & a_{1n} b_{2q} \\
   \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots & & & \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\
   a_{11} b_{p1} & a_{11} b_{p2} & \cdots & a_{11} b_{pq} &
                   \cdots & \cdots & a_{1n} b_{p1} & a_{1n} b_{p2} & \cdots & a_{1n} b_{pq} \\
   \vdots & \vdots & & \vdots & \ddots & & \vdots & \vdots & & \vdots \\
   \vdots & \vdots & & \vdots & & \ddots & \vdots & \vdots & & \vdots \\
   a_{m1} b_{11} & a_{m1} b_{12} & \cdots & a_{m1} b_{1q} &
                   \cdots & \cdots & a_{mn} b_{11} & a_{mn} b_{12} & \cdots & a_{mn} b_{1q} \\
   a_{m1} b_{21} & a_{m1} b_{22} & \cdots & a_{m1} b_{2q} &
                   \cdots & \cdots & a_{mn} b_{21} & a_{mn} b_{22} & \cdots & a_{mn} b_{2q} \\
   \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots & & & \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\
   a_{m1} b_{p1} & a_{m1} b_{p2} & \cdots & a_{m1} b_{pq} &
                   \cdots & \cdots & a_{mn} b_{p1} & a_{mn} b_{p2} & \cdots & a_{mn} b_{pq}
\end{bmatrix}. </math>

Using <math>/\!/</math> and <math>\%</math> to denote [[truncating integer division]] and [[remainder]], respectively, and numbering the matrix elements starting from 0, one obtains 
: <math>(A\otimes B)_{pr+v, qs+w} = a_{rs} b_{vw}</math> 
: <math>(A\otimes B)_{i, j} = a_{i /\!/ p, j /\!/ q} b_{i \%p, j \% q}.</math> 
For the usual numbering starting from 1, one obtains
: <math>
(A\otimes B)_{p(r-1)+v, q(s-1)+w} = a_{rs} b_{vw}
</math>
: <math>
(A\otimes B)_{i, j} = a_{\lceil i/p \rceil,\lceil j/q \rceil} b_{((i-1)\%p) +1, ((j-1)\%q) + 1}.
</math>

If '''A''' and '''B''' represent [[linear transformations]] {{nowrap|'''V'''<sub>1</sub> → '''W'''<sub>1</sub>}} and {{nowrap|'''V'''<sub>2</sub> → '''W'''<sub>2</sub>}}, respectively, then the [[tensor product]] of the two maps is a map {{nowrap|'''V'''<sub>1</sub> &otimes; '''V'''<sub>2</sub> → '''W'''<sub>1</sub> &otimes; '''W'''<sub>2</sub>}} represented by {{nowrap|'''A''' &otimes; '''B'''}}.

=== Examples ===
: <math>
  \begin{bmatrix}
    1 & 2 \\
    3 & 4 \\
  \end{bmatrix} \otimes
  \begin{bmatrix}
    0 & 5 \\
    6 & 7 \\
  \end{bmatrix} =
  \begin{bmatrix}
    1 \begin{bmatrix}
      0 & 5 \\
      6 & 7 \\
    \end{bmatrix} & 
    2 \begin{bmatrix}
      0 & 5 \\
      6 & 7 \\
    \end{bmatrix} \\

    3 \begin{bmatrix}
      0 & 5 \\
      6 & 7 \\
    \end{bmatrix} & 
    4 \begin{bmatrix}
      0 & 5 \\
      6 & 7 \\
    \end{bmatrix} \\
  \end{bmatrix} =

  \left[\begin{array}{cc|cc}
    1\times 0 & 1\times 5 & 2\times 0 & 2\times 5 \\
    1\times 6 & 1\times 7 & 2\times 6 & 2\times 7 \\ \hline
    3\times 0 & 3\times 5 & 4\times 0 & 4\times 5 \\
    3\times 6 & 3\times 7 & 4\times 6 & 4\times 7 \\
  \end{array}\right] =

  \left[\begin{array}{cc|cc}
     0 &  5 &  0 & 10 \\
     6 &  7 & 12 & 14 \\ \hline
     0 & 15 &  0 & 20 \\
    18 & 21 & 24 & 28
  \end{array}\right].
</math>

Similarly:

: <math>
\begin{bmatrix}
1 & -4 & 7 \\
-2 & 3 & 3
\end{bmatrix} \otimes
\begin{bmatrix}
8 & -9 & -6 & 5 \\
1 & -3 & -4 & 7 \\
2 & 8 & -8 & -3 \\
1 & 2 & -5 & -1
\end{bmatrix} =
\left[\begin{array}{cccc|cccc|cccc}
8 & -9 & -6 & 5 & -32 & 36 & 24 & -20 & 56 & -63 & -42 & 35 \\
1 & -3 & -4 & 7 & -4 & 12 & 16 & -28 & 7 & -21 & -28 & 49 \\
2 & 8 & -8 & -3 & -8 & -32 & 32 & 12 & 14 & 56 & -56 & -21 \\
1 & 2 & -5 & -1 & -4 & -8 & 20 & 4 & 7 & 14 & -35 & -7 \\ \hline
-16 & 18 & 12 & -10 & 24 & -27 & -18 & 15 & 24 & -27 & -18 & 15 \\
-2 & 6 & 8 & -14 & 3 & -9 & -12 & 21 & 3 & -9 & -12 & 21 \\
-4 & -16 & 16 & 6 & 6 & 24 & -24 & -9 & 6 & 24 & -24 & -9 \\
-2 & -4 & 10 & 2 & 3 & 6 & -15 & -3 & 3 & 6 & -15 & -3
\end{array}\right]
</math>

== Properties ==
=== Relations to other matrix operations ===
{{ordered list
| 1 = '''[[Bilinearity]] and [[associativity]]:'''{{paragraph}}

The Kronecker product is a special case of the [[tensor product]], so it is [[bilinear operator|bilinear]] and [[associativity|associative]]:

: <math>\begin{align}
        \mathbf{A} \otimes (\mathbf{B} + \mathbf{C}) &= \mathbf{A} \otimes \mathbf{B} + \mathbf{A} \otimes \mathbf{C}, \\
        (\mathbf{B} + \mathbf{C}) \otimes \mathbf{A} &= \mathbf{B} \otimes \mathbf{A} + \mathbf{C} \otimes \mathbf{A}, \\
                    (k\mathbf{A}) \otimes \mathbf{B} &= \mathbf{A} \otimes (k\mathbf{B}) = k(\mathbf{A} \otimes \mathbf{B}), \\
  (\mathbf{A} \otimes \mathbf{B}) \otimes \mathbf{C} &= \mathbf{A} \otimes (\mathbf{B} \otimes \mathbf{C}), \\
  \mathbf{A} \otimes \mathbf{0} &= \mathbf{0} \otimes \mathbf{A} = \mathbf{0},
\end{align}</math>

where '''A''', '''B''' and '''C''' are matrices, '''0''' is a zero matrix, and ''k'' is a scalar.
| 2 = '''Non-[[commutative operation|commutative]]:'''{{paragraph}}

In general, {{nowrap|'''A''' &otimes; '''B'''}} and {{nowrap|'''B''' &otimes; '''A'''}} are different matrices. However, {{nowrap|'''A''' &otimes; '''B'''}} and {{nowrap|'''B''' &otimes; '''A'''}} are permutation equivalent, meaning that there exist [[permutation matrix|permutation matrices]] '''P''' and '''Q''' such that<ref>
{{cite journal
 | first1 = H.V.  | last1 = Henderson
 | first2 = S.R.  | last2 = Searle
 | year = 1980
 | title = The vec-permutation matrix, the vec operator and Kronecker products: A review
 | journal = Linear and Multilinear Algebra
 | volume = 9  | number = 4  | pages = 271–288
 | doi = 10.1080/03081088108817379  | hdl = 1813/32747
 | url = https://ecommons.cornell.edu/bitstream/1813/32747/1/BU-645-M.pdf
| hdl-access = free
 }}
</ref>
: <math> \mathbf{B} \otimes \mathbf{A} = \mathbf{P} \, \left(\mathbf{A} \otimes \mathbf{B}\right) \, \mathbf{Q}. </math>
If '''A''' and '''B''' are square, then {{nowrap|'''A''' &otimes; '''B'''}} and {{nowrap|'''B''' &otimes; '''A'''}} are even permutation [[Similar matrix|similar]], meaning that we can take {{nowrap|'''P''' {{=}} '''Q'''<sup>T</sup>}}.

The matrices {{nowrap|'''P'''}} and {{nowrap|'''Q'''}} are perfect shuffle matrices, called the "commutation" matrix.<ref>
{{cite journal
 | first = Charles F.  | last = Van Loan
 | year = 2000
 | title = The ubiquitous Kronecker product
 | journal = [[Journal of Computational and Applied Mathematics]]
 | volume = 123  | number = 1–2  | pages = 85–100
 | doi = 10.1016/s0377-0427(00)00393-9  | doi-access = free
 | bibcode = 2000JCoAM.123...85L
}}
</ref> The Commutation matrix '''S'''<sub>''p'',&nbsp;''q''</sub> can be constructed by taking slices of the '''I'''<sub>''r''</sub> identity matrix, where <math>r=pq</math>.

: <math>\mathbf{S}_{p,q} = \begin{bmatrix}
  \mathbf{I}_r(1:q:r,:) \\ 
  \mathbf{I}_r(2:q:r,:) \\ 
  \vdots \\
  \mathbf{I}_r(q:q:r,:)
\end{bmatrix}</math>

[[MATLAB]] colon notation is used here to indicate submatrices, and '''I'''<sub>''r''</sub> is the {{nowrap|''r'' × ''r''}} identity matrix. If <math>\mathbf{A} \in \mathbb{R}^{m_1 \times n_1}</math> and <math>\mathbf{B} \in \mathbb{R}^{m_2 \times n_2}</math>, then

: <math>\mathbf{B} \otimes \mathbf{A} = \mathbf{S}_{m_1,m_2} (\mathbf{A} \otimes \mathbf{B}) \mathbf{S}^\textsf{T}_{n_1,n_2}</math>
| 3 = '''The mixed-product property:'''{{paragraph}}

If '''A''', '''B''', '''C''' and '''D''' are matrices of such size that one can form the [[matrix product]]s '''AC''' and '''BD''', then<ref name="liu5">{{Cite journal| last1=Liu|first1=Shuangzhe|
last2= Trenkler|first2=Götz| last3=Kollo|first3=Tõnu| 
last4=von Rosen|first4=Dietrich| 
last5=Baksalary|first5=Oskar Maria| 
date= 2023|
title= Professor Heinz Neudecker and matrix differential calculus| 
journal= Statistical Papers|volume=65 |issue=4 |pages=2605–2639 | language=en|
doi= 10.1007/s00362-023-01499-w}}</ref>
: <math> (\mathbf{A} \otimes \mathbf{B})(\mathbf{C} \otimes \mathbf{D}) = (\mathbf{AC}) \otimes (\mathbf{BD}). </math>

This is called the ''mixed-product property'', because it mixes the ordinary matrix product and the Kronecker product.

As an immediate consequence (again, taking <math>\mathbf{A} \in \mathbb{R}^{m_1 \times n_1}</math> and <math>\mathbf{B} \in \mathbb{R}^{m_2 \times n_2}</math>),

: <math>\mathbf{A} \otimes \mathbf{B} = (\mathbf{I}_{m_1} \otimes \mathbf{B} )(\mathbf{A} \otimes \mathbf{I}_{n_2}) = (\mathbf{A} \otimes \mathbf{I}_{m_2} )(\mathbf{I}_{n_1} \otimes \mathbf{B}) . </math>

In particular, using the ''transpose'' property from below, this means that if 
: <math> \mathbf{A} = \mathbf{Q} \otimes \mathbf{U}</math>
and '''Q''' and '''U''' are [[Orthogonal matrix|orthogonal]] (or [[Unitary matrix|unitary]]), then '''A''' is also orthogonal (resp., unitary).

The mixed Kronecker matrix-vector product can be written as:

: <math>
\left( \mathbf{A} \otimes \mathbf{B} \right) \operatorname{vec} \left( \mathbf{V} \right) = \operatorname{vec} (\mathbf{B} \mathbf{V} \mathbf{A}^T)
</math>

where <math> \operatorname{vec}(\mathbf{V})</math> is the [[Vectorization (mathematics)|vectorization]] operator applied on <math>\mathbf{V}</math> (formed by reshaping the matrix).
| 4 = '''[[Commutator#Ring theory|Commutator property]]:'''{{paragraph}}

If <math>\mathbf{A}</math> and <math>\mathbf{C}</math> are square matrices of the dimension <math>m</math>, and <math>\mathbf{B}</math> and <math>\mathbf{D}</math> are square matrices of the dimension <math>n</math>, then the commutator
: <math>[\mathbf{A} \otimes \mathbf{B},\mathbf{C} \otimes \mathbf{D}]=[\mathbf{A},\mathbf{C}]\otimes (\mathbf{B}\mathbf{D}) +  (\mathbf{C}\mathbf{A}) \otimes [\mathbf{B},\mathbf{D}]</math>,
or
: <math>[\mathbf{A} \otimes \mathbf{B},\mathbf{C} \otimes \mathbf{D}]=[\mathbf{A},\mathbf{C}]\otimes (\mathbf{D}\mathbf{B}) +  (\mathbf{A}\mathbf{C}) \otimes [\mathbf{B},\mathbf{D}]</math>.

| 5 = '''[[Hadamard product (matrices)|Hadamard product]] (element-wise multiplication):'''{{paragraph}}

The mixed-product property also works for the element-wise product. If '''A''' and '''C''' are matrices of the same size, '''B''' and '''D''' are matrices of the same size, then<ref name="liu5" />
: <math> (\mathbf{A} \otimes \mathbf{B}) \circ (\mathbf{C} \otimes \mathbf{D}) = (\mathbf{A} \circ \mathbf{C}) \otimes (\mathbf{B} \circ \mathbf{D}). </math>
| 6 = '''The inverse of a Kronecker product:'''{{paragraph}}

It follows that {{nowrap|'''A''' &otimes; '''B'''}} is [[invertible matrix|invertible]] [[if and only if]] both '''A''' and '''B''' are invertible, in which case the inverse is given by
: <math> (\mathbf{A} \otimes \mathbf{B})^{-1} = \mathbf{A}^{-1} \otimes \mathbf{B}^{-1}. </math>

The invertible product property holds for the [[Moore–Penrose pseudoinverse]] as well,<ref name="liu5" /><ref>{{cite journal
 |last1=Langville  |first1=Amy N.  |author1-link=Amy Langville
 |last2=Stewart    |first2=William J.
 |date=1 June 2004
 |title=The Kronecker product and stochastic automata networks
 |journal=Journal of Computational and Applied Mathematics
 |volume=167  |issue=2  |pages=429–447
 |doi=10.1016/j.cam.2003.10.010  |doi-access=free
 |bibcode=2004JCoAM.167..429L
}}</ref><ref name="Sliu2025">{{cite journal
 |last1=Liu |first1=Shuangzhe
 |last2=Wang |first2=Hongxing
 |last3=Liu |first3=Yonghui
 |last4=Liu |first4=Conan
 |year=2024
 |title=Matrix derivatives and Kronecker products for the core and generalized core inverses
 |journal=Journal of Mathematical Analysis and Applications
 |volume=535
 |issue=1
 |article-number=128128
 |doi= 10.1016/j.jmaa.2024.128128
}}</ref>
that is
: <math> (\mathbf{A} \otimes \mathbf{B})^{+} = \mathbf{A}^{+} \otimes \mathbf{B}^{+}. </math>

In the language of [[category theory]], the mixed-product property of the Kronecker product (and more general tensor product) shows that the category '''Mat'''<sub>''F''</sub> of matrices over a [[field (mathematics)|field]] ''F'' is in fact a [[monoidal category]], with objects natural numbers ''n'', morphisms {{nowrap|''n'' → ''m''}} are {{nowrap|''n'' × ''m''}} matrices with entries in ''F'', composition is given by matrix multiplication, [[identity arrows]] are simply {{nowrap|''n'' × ''n''}} [[identity matrices]] ''I<sub>n</sub>'', and the tensor product is given by the Kronecker product.<ref>
{{cite journal
 |last1 = Macedo   |first1 = Hugo Daniel
 |last2 = Oliveira |first2 = José Nuno
 |year = 2013
 |title = Typing linear algebra: A biproduct-oriented approach
 |journal = [[Science of Computer Programming]]
 |volume = 78  |issue = 11  |pages = 2160–2191
 |arxiv = 1312.4818
 |bibcode = 2013arXiv1312.4818M   |s2cid = 9846072
 |doi = 10.1016/j.scico.2012.07.012
}}
</ref>

'''Mat'''<sub>''F''</sub> is a concrete [[Skeleton (category theory)|skeleton category]] for the [[equivalence of categories|equivalent category]] '''FinVect'''<sub>''F''</sub> of finite dimensional vector spaces over ''F'', whose objects are such finite dimensional vector spaces ''V'', arrows are ''F''-linear maps {{nowrap|''L'' : ''V'' → ''W''}}, and identity arrows are the identity maps of the spaces. The equivalence of categories amounts to simultaneously [[axiom of choice|choosing a basis]] in every finite-dimensional vector space ''V'' over ''F''; matrices' elements represent these mappings with respect to the chosen bases; and likewise the Kronecker product is the representation of the [[tensor product]] in the chosen bases.
| 7 = '''[[Transpose]]:'''{{paragraph}}

Transposition and [[conjugate transpose|conjugate transposition]] are distributive over the Kronecker product:
: <math>(\mathbf{A}\otimes \mathbf{B})^\textsf{T} = \mathbf{A}^\textsf{T} \otimes \mathbf{B}^\textsf{T}</math> and <math>(\mathbf{A}\otimes \mathbf{B})^* = \mathbf{A}^* \otimes \mathbf{B}^*.</math>
| 8 = '''[[Determinant]]:'''{{paragraph}}

Let '''A''' be an {{nowrap|''n'' × ''n''}} matrix and let '''B''' be an {{nowrap|''m'' × ''m''}} matrix. Then
: <math> \left| \mathbf{A} \otimes \mathbf{B} \right| = \left| \mathbf{A} \right| ^m \left| \mathbf{B} \right| ^n .</math>
The exponent in {{abs|'''A'''}} is the order of '''B''' and the exponent in {{abs|'''B'''}} is the order of '''A'''.
| 9 = '''Kronecker sum and [[Matrix exponential|exponentiation]]:'''{{Anchor|Kronecker sum}}{{paragraph}}

If '''A''' is {{nowrap|''n'' × ''n''}}, '''B''' is {{nowrap|''m'' × ''m''}}, and '''I'''<sub>''k''</sub> denotes the {{nowrap|''k'' × ''k''}} [[identity matrix]] then we can define what is sometimes called the '''Kronecker sum''', {{overline|&oplus;}}, by
: <math> \mathbf{A}\,\overline{\oplus}\,\mathbf{B} = \mathbf{A} \otimes \mathbf{I}_m + \mathbf{I}_n \otimes \mathbf{B} .</math>

This is ''different'' from the [[Direct_sum_of_matrices|''direct sum'']] of two matrices. This operation is related to the tensor product on [[Lie algebra]]s, as detailed below ([[#Abstract properties]]) in the point "Relation to the abstract [[tensor product]]".

We have the following formula for the [[matrix exponential]], which is useful in some numerical evaluations.<ref>
{{cite journal
 | first = J.W.  | last = Brewer
 | year = 1969
 | title = A note on Kronecker matrix products and matrix equation systems
 | journal = [[SIAM Journal on Applied Mathematics]]
 | volume = 17  | number = 3  | pages = 603–606
 | doi = 10.1137/0117057
}}
</ref>

: <math>  \exp({\mathbf{N}\,\overline{\oplus}\,\mathbf{M}}) = \exp(\mathbf{N}) \otimes \exp(\mathbf{M}) </math>

Kronecker sums appear naturally in [[physics]] when considering ensembles of non-interacting [[Physical system|systems]].{{Citation needed | reason=some may want to know more about the details of this | date= October 2014}}

If ''H<sup>r</sup>'' is the Hamiltonian of the ''r''th such system. Then the total Hamiltonian of the ensemble is
: <math>H_{\operatorname{Tot}}=\overline{\bigoplus_r} H^r .</math>
| 10 = '''[[Vectorization (mathematics)|Vectorization]] of a Kronecker product:'''{{paragraph}}
Let <math>A</math> be an <math>m\times n</math> matrix and <math>B</math> a <math>p \times q</math> matrix. When the order of the Kronecker product and vectorization is interchanged, the two operations can be linked linearly through a function that involves the [[commutation matrix]], <math>K_{qm} </math>. That is, <math>\operatorname{vec}(\operatorname{Kron}(A, B))</math> and <math>\operatorname{Kron}(\operatorname{vec}A,\operatorname{vec}B)</math> have the following relationship:

: <math>\operatorname{vec}(A\otimes B) = (I_n \otimes K_{qm}\otimes I_p)(\operatorname{vec}A \otimes \operatorname{vec}B). </math>

Furthermore, the above relation can be rearranged in terms of either <math>\operatorname{vec}A</math> or <math>\operatorname{vec}B</math> as follows:

: <math>\operatorname{vec}(A\otimes B)= (I_n \otimes G)\operatorname{vec}A = (H\otimes I_p)\operatorname{vec}B, </math>

where 
: <math>G = (K_{qm}\otimes I_p)(I_m \otimes \operatorname{vec}B) \text{ and } H=(I_n\otimes K_{qm})(\operatorname{vec}A \otimes I_q). </math>
| 11 = '''[[Outer Product]]:'''{{paragraph}}
If <math>x \in \mathbb{R}^n</math> and <math>y \in \mathbb{R}^m</math> are arbitrary vectors, then the outer product between <math>x</math> and <math>y</math> is defined as <math>xy^T</math>. The Kronecker product is related to the outer product by: <math>y\otimes x = \operatorname{vec}(xy^T)</math>.
}}

=== Abstract properties ===
{{ordered list
|1= '''[[Spectrum (functional analysis)|Spectrum]]:'''{{paragraph}}

Suppose that '''A''' and '''B''' are square matrices of size ''n'' and ''m'' respectively. Let ''λ''<sub>1</sub>, ..., ''λ''<sub>''n''</sub> be the [[eigenvalue]]s of '''A''' and ''μ''<sub>1</sub>, ..., ''μ''<sub>''m''</sub> be those of '''B''' (listed according to [[multiplicity (mathematics)|multiplicity]]). Then the [[eigenvalues]] of {{nowrap|'''A''' &otimes; '''B'''}} are
: <math> \lambda_i \mu_j, \qquad i=1,\ldots,n ,\, j=1,\ldots,m. </math>

It follows that the [[trace (matrix)|trace]] and [[determinant]] of a Kronecker product are given by
: <math> \operatorname{tr}(\mathbf{A} \otimes \mathbf{B}) = \operatorname{tr} \mathbf{A} \, \operatorname{tr} \mathbf{B} \quad\text{and}\quad \det(\mathbf{A} \otimes \mathbf{B}) = (\det \mathbf{A})^m (\det \mathbf{B})^n. </math>

|2= '''[[singular value decomposition|Singular values]]:'''{{paragraph}}

If '''A''' and '''B''' are rectangular matrices, then one can consider their [[singular value decomposition|singular values]]. Suppose that '''A''' has ''r''<sub>'''A'''</sub> nonzero singular values, namely
: <math> \sigma_{\mathbf{A},i}, \qquad i = 1, \ldots, r_\mathbf{A}. </math>

Similarly, denote the nonzero singular values of '''B''' by
: <math> \sigma_{\mathbf{B},i}, \qquad i = 1, \ldots, r_\mathbf{B}. </math>

Then the Kronecker product {{nowrap|'''A''' &otimes; '''B'''}} has ''r''<sub>'''A'''</sub>''r''<sub>'''B'''</sub> nonzero singular values, namely
: <math> \sigma_{\mathbf{A},i} \sigma_{\mathbf{B},j}, \qquad i=1,\ldots,r_\mathbf{A} ,\, j=1,\ldots,r_\mathbf{B}. </math>

Since the [[rank of a matrix]] equals the number of nonzero singular values, we find that
: <math> \operatorname{rank}(\mathbf{A} \otimes \mathbf{B}) = \operatorname{rank} \mathbf{A} \, \operatorname{rank} \mathbf{B}. </math>

|3= '''Relation to the abstract [[tensor product]]:'''{{paragraph}}

The Kronecker product of matrices corresponds to the abstract tensor product of linear maps. Specifically, if the vector spaces ''V'', ''W'', ''X'', and ''Y'' have bases {{nowrap|{''v''<sub>1</sub>, ..., ''v''<sub>''m''</sub>},}} {{nowrap|{''w''<sub>1</sub>, ..., ''w''<sub>''n''</sub>},}} {{nowrap|{''x''<sub>1</sub>, ..., ''x''<sub>''d''</sub>},}} and {{nowrap|{''y''<sub>1</sub>, ..., ''y''<sub>''e''</sub>},}} respectively, and if the matrices ''A'' and ''B'' represent the linear transformations {{nowrap|''S'' : ''V'' → ''X''}} and {{nowrap|''T'' : ''W'' → ''Y''}}, respectively in the appropriate bases, then the matrix {{nowrap|''A'' &otimes; ''B''}} represents the tensor product of the two maps, {{nowrap|''S'' &otimes; ''T'' : ''V'' &otimes; ''W'' → ''X'' &otimes; ''Y''}} with respect to the basis {{nowrap|{''v''<sub>1</sub> &otimes; ''w''<sub>1</sub>, ''v''<sub>1</sub> &otimes; ''w''<sub>2</sub>, ..., ''v''<sub>2</sub> &otimes; ''w''<sub>1</sub>, ..., ''v''<sub>''m''</sub> &otimes; ''w''<sub>''n''</sub>}{{void}}}} of {{nowrap|''V'' &otimes; ''W''}} and the similarly defined basis of {{nowrap|''X'' &otimes; ''Y''}} with the property that {{nowrap|1=''A'' &otimes; ''B''(''v''<sub>''i''</sub> &otimes; ''w''<sub>''j''</sub>) = (''Av''<sub>''i''</sub>) &otimes; (''Bw''<sub>''j''</sub>)}}, where ''i'' and ''j'' are integers in the proper range.<ref>
{{cite book
 | last1=Dummit | first1=David S.
 | last2=Foote  | first2=Richard M.
 | year=1999
 | title=Abstract Algebra  | edition=2  | pages=401–402
 | publisher=John Wiley and Sons  | location=New York
 | isbn=978-0-471-36857-1
}}
</ref>

When ''V'' and ''W'' are [[Lie algebra]]s, and {{nowrap|''S'' : ''V'' → ''V''}} and {{nowrap|''T'' : ''W'' → ''W''}} are [[Lie algebra homomorphism]]s, the Kronecker sum of ''A'' and ''B'' represents the induced Lie algebra homomorphisms {{nowrap|''V'' &otimes; ''W'' → ''V'' &otimes; ''W''}}.{{Citation needed|date=July 2023}}

|4= '''Relation to [[graph product|products of graphs]]:'''{{paragraph}}

The Kronecker product of the [[adjacency matrix|adjacency matrices]] of two [[Graph (discrete mathematics)|graphs]] is the adjacency matrix of the [[tensor product of graphs|tensor product graph]]. The [[Kronecker product#Kronecker sum and exponentiation|Kronecker sum]] of the adjacency matrices of two [[Graph (discrete mathematics)|graphs]] is the adjacency matrix of the [[cartesian product of graphs|Cartesian product graph]].<ref name="TAOCP0a">See {{cite web
 |first=D.E.
 |last=Knuth |author-link=Donald Knuth
 |title=Pre-Fascicle 0a: Introduction to Combinatorial Algorithms
 |edition=zeroth printing, revision&nbsp;2
 |at=answer to Exercise&nbsp;96
 |url=http://www-cs-faculty.stanford.edu/~knuth/fasc0a.ps.gz
 |postscript=,
 |access-date=2007-10-24
 |archive-date=2019-05-13
 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190513215832/http://www-cs-faculty.stanford.edu/~knuth/fasc0a.ps.gz
 }} to appear as part of {{cite book
 |first=D.E. |last=Knuth
 |title=[[The Art of Computer Programming]]
 |volume=4A
}}</ref>
}}

== Matrix equations ==
The Kronecker product can be used to get a convenient representation for some matrix equations. Consider for instance the equation {{nowrap|1='''AXB''' = '''C'''}}, where '''A''', '''B''' and '''C''' are given matrices and the matrix '''X''' is the unknown. We can use the "vec trick" to rewrite this equation as
: <math>
    \left(\mathbf{B}^\textsf{T} \otimes \mathbf{A}\right) \, \operatorname{vec}(\mathbf{X})
  = \operatorname{vec}(\mathbf{AXB}) = \operatorname{vec}(\mathbf{C})
.</math>

Here, vec('''X''') denotes the [[vectorization (mathematics)|vectorization]] of the matrix '''X''', formed by stacking the columns of '''X''' into a single [[column vector]].

It now follows from the properties of the Kronecker product that the equation {{nowrap|1='''AXB''' = '''C'''}} has a unique solution, if and only if '''A''' and '''B''' are invertible {{harv|Horn|Johnson|1991|loc=Lemma 4.3.1}}.

If '''X''' and '''C''' are row-ordered into the column vectors '''u''' and '''v''', respectively, then {{harv|Jain|1989|loc=2.8 Block Matrices and Kronecker Products}}
: <math>
  \mathbf{v} = 
  \left(\mathbf{A} \otimes \mathbf{B}^\textsf{T}\right)\mathbf{u}
.</math>

The reason is that
: <math>
  \mathbf{v} = 
  \operatorname{vec}\left((\mathbf{AXB})^\textsf{T}\right) = 
  \operatorname{vec}\left(\mathbf{B}^\textsf{T}\mathbf{X}^\textsf{T}\mathbf{A}^\textsf{T}\right) = 
  \left(\mathbf{A} \otimes \mathbf{B}^\textsf{T}\right)\operatorname{vec}\left(\mathbf{X^\textsf{T}}\right) = 
  \left(\mathbf{A} \otimes \mathbf{B}^\textsf{T}\right)\mathbf{u}
.</math>

=== Applications ===
For an example of the application of this formula, see the article on the [[Lyapunov equation]]. This formula also comes in handy in showing that the [[matrix normal distribution]] is a special case of the [[multivariate normal distribution]]. This formula is also useful for representing 2D [[image processing]] operations in matrix-vector form.

Another example is when a matrix can be factored as a Kronecker product, then matrix multiplication can be performed faster by using the above formula. This can be applied recursively, as done in the [[Cooley–Tukey FFT algorithm#The radix-2 DIT case|radix-2 FFT]] and the [[Fast Walsh–Hadamard transform]]. Splitting a known matrix into the Kronecker product of two smaller matrices is known as the "nearest Kronecker product" problem, and can be solved exactly<ref name="VanLoan">
{{cite book
 |last1=Van Loan  |first1=C.
 |last2=Pitsianis |first2=N.
 |year=1992
 |title=Approximation with Kronecker Products
 |publisher=Cornell University Press
 |location=Ithaca, NY
}}
</ref> by using the [[Singular value decomposition|SVD]]. To split a matrix into the Kronecker product of more than two matrices, in an optimal fashion, is a difficult problem and the subject of ongoing research; some authors cast it as a tensor decomposition problem.<ref>
{{cite book
|doi=10.1109/SMC.2016.7844903
|chapter=Kronecker product approximation with multiple factor matrices via the tensor product algorithm
|title=2016 IEEE International Conference on Systems, Man, and Cybernetics (SMC)
|pages=004277–004282
|year=2016
|last1=King Keung Wu
|last2=Yam|first2=Yeung
|last3=Meng|first3=Helen|author3-link=Helen Meng
|last4=Mesbahi|first4=Mehran
|isbn=978-1-5090-1897-0
|s2cid=30695585
}}
</ref><ref>
{{cite book
 |last1=Dantas    |first1=Cássio F.
 |last2=Cohen     |first2=Jérémy E.
 |last3=Gribonval |first3=Rémi
 |chapter=Learning Fast Dictionaries for Sparse Representations Using Low-Rank Tensor Decompositions
 |year=2018
 |title=Latent Variable Analysis and Signal Separation
 |series=Lecture Notes in Computer Science
 |volume=10891  |pages=456–466
 |doi=10.1007/978-3-319-93764-9_42
 |isbn=978-3-319-93763-2
 |s2cid=46963798
 |chapter-url=https://hal.inria.fr/hal-01709343v2/document
 |url=https://hal.inria.fr/hal-01709343/file/notes%20%281%29.pdf
}}
</ref>

In conjunction with the [[least squares|least squares method]], the Kronecker product can be used as an accurate solution to the [[hand–eye calibration problem]].<ref>
{{cite journal
 |first1=Algo  |last1=Li
 |display-authors=etal
 |date=4 September 2010
 |title=Simultaneous robot-world and hand-eye calibration using dual-quaternions and Kronecker product.
 |journal=International Journal of the Physical Sciences
 |volume=5 |issue=10 |pages=1530–1536
 |s2cid=7446157
 |url=https://pdfs.semanticscholar.org/225d/e4ea2d3f18b7743bfeabf925fa603fc47bcb.pdf  |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200209164546/https://pdfs.semanticscholar.org/225d/e4ea2d3f18b7743bfeabf925fa603fc47bcb.pdf  |archive-date=9 February 2020  }}
</ref>

== Related matrix operations {{Anchor|Tracy–Singh and [[Khatri–Rao product]]s}} ==
Two related matrix operations are the '''Tracy–Singh''' and '''[[Khatri–Rao product]]s''', which operate on [[Block matrix|partitioned matrices]]. Let the {{nowrap|''m'' × ''n''}} matrix '''A''' be partitioned into the {{nowrap|''m''<sub>''i''</sub> × ''n''<sub>''j''</sub>}} blocks '''A'''<sub>''ij''</sub> and {{nowrap|''p'' × ''q''}} matrix '''B''' into the {{nowrap|''p<sub>k</sub>'' × ''q<sub>{{ell}}</sub>''}} blocks '''B'''<sub>''kl''</sub>, with of course {{nowrap|1=Σ''<sub>i</sub> m<sub>i</sub>'' = ''m''}}, {{nowrap|1=Σ''<sub>j</sub> n<sub>j</sub>'' = ''n''}}, {{nowrap|1=Σ''<sub>k</sub> p<sub>k</sub>'' = ''p''}} and {{nowrap|1=Σ''<sub>{{ell}}</sub> q<sub>{{ell}}</sub>'' = ''q''}}.

=== Tracy–Singh product ===
The '''Tracy–Singh product''' is defined as<ref>
{{cite journal
 |last1=Tracy |first1=D.S.
 |last2=Singh |first2=R.P.
 |year=1972
 |title=A new matrix product and its applications in matrix differentiation
 |journal=[[Statistica Neerlandica]]
 |volume=26  |issue=4  |pages=143–157
 |doi=10.1111/j.1467-9574.1972.tb00199.x
}}
</ref><ref>
{{cite journal
 |last=Liu|first=Shuangzhe
 |year=1999
 |title=Matrix Results on the Khatri–Rao and Tracy–Singh Products
 |journal=Linear Algebra and Its Applications
 |volume=289 |issue=1–3 |pages=267–277
 |doi=10.1016/S0024-3795(98)10209-4 |doi-access=free }}
</ref><ref>
{{cite journal
|last1=Liu |first1=Shuangzhe|last2=Trenkler |first2=Götz
|year=2008
|title= Hadamard, Khatri-Rao, Kronecker and other matrix products
|journal= International Journal of Information and Systems Sciences
 |volume=4 |issue=1 |pages=160–177}}
</ref>
: <math>\mathbf{A} \circ \mathbf{B} = \left(\mathbf{A}_{ij} \circ \mathbf{B}\right)_{ij} = \left(\left(\mathbf{A}_{ij} \otimes \mathbf{B}_{kl}\right)_{kl}\right)_{ij}</math>

which means that the (''ij'')-th subblock of the {{nowrap|''mp'' × ''nq''}} product {{nowrap|'''A''' <math>\circ</math> '''B'''}} is the {{nowrap|''m<sub>i</sub> p'' × ''n<sub>j</sub> q''}} matrix {{nowrap|'''A'''<sub>''ij''</sub> <math>\circ</math> '''B'''}}, of which the (''k{{ell}}'')-th subblock equals the {{nowrap|''m<sub>i</sub> p<sub>k</sub>'' × ''n<sub>j</sub> q<sub>{{ell}}</sub>''}} matrix {{nowrap|'''A'''<sub>''ij''</sub> &otimes; '''B'''<sub>''k{{ell}}''</sub>}}. Essentially the Tracy–Singh product is the pairwise Kronecker product for each pair of partitions in the two matrices.

For example, if '''A''' and '''B''' both are {{nowrap|2 × 2}} partitioned matrices e.g.:
: <math> \mathbf{A} = 
\left[
\begin{array} {c | c}
\mathbf{A}_{11} & \mathbf{A}_{12} \\
\hline
\mathbf{A}_{21} & \mathbf{A}_{22}
\end{array}
\right]
= 
\left[
\begin{array} {c c | c}
1 & 2 & 3 \\
4 & 5 & 6 \\
\hline
7 & 8 & 9
\end{array}
\right]
,\quad
\mathbf{B} = 
\left[
\begin{array} {c | c}
\mathbf{B}_{11} & \mathbf{B}_{12} \\
\hline
\mathbf{B}_{21} & \mathbf{B}_{22}
\end{array}
\right]
= 
\left[
\begin{array} {c | c c}
1 & 4 & 7 \\
\hline
2 & 5 & 8 \\
3 & 6 & 9
\end{array}
\right]
,
</math>

we get:
: <math>\begin{align}
  \mathbf{A} \circ \mathbf{B} 
  ={}& \left[\begin{array} {c | c}
      \mathbf{A}_{11} \circ \mathbf{B} & \mathbf{A}_{12} \circ \mathbf{B} \\
      \hline
      \mathbf{A}_{21} \circ \mathbf{B} & \mathbf{A}_{22} \circ \mathbf{B}
    \end{array}\right] \\
  ={} &\left[\begin{array} {c | c | c | c}
         \mathbf{A}_{11} \otimes \mathbf{B}_{11} & \mathbf{A}_{11} \otimes \mathbf{B}_{12} & \mathbf{A}_{12} \otimes \mathbf{B}_{11} & \mathbf{A}_{12} \otimes \mathbf{B}_{12} \\
         \hline
         \mathbf{A}_{11} \otimes \mathbf{B}_{21} & \mathbf{A}_{11} \otimes \mathbf{B}_{22} & \mathbf{A}_{12} \otimes \mathbf{B}_{21} & \mathbf{A}_{12} \otimes \mathbf{B}_{22} \\
         \hline
         \mathbf{A}_{21} \otimes \mathbf{B}_{11} & \mathbf{A}_{21} \otimes \mathbf{B}_{12} & \mathbf{A}_{22}          \otimes \mathbf{B}_{11} & \mathbf{A}_{22} \otimes \mathbf{B}_{12} \\
         \hline
         \mathbf{A}_{21} \otimes \mathbf{B}_{21} & \mathbf{A}_{21} \otimes \mathbf{B}_{22} & \mathbf{A}_{22} \otimes \mathbf{B}_{21} & \mathbf{A}_{22} \otimes \mathbf{B}_{22}
  \end{array}\right] \\
  ={} &\left[\begin{array} {c c | c c c c | c | c c}
          1 &  2 &  4 &  7 &  8 & 14 &  3 & 12 & 21 \\
          4 &  5 & 16 & 28 & 20 & 35 &  6 & 24 & 42 \\
          \hline
          2 &  4 &  5 &  8 & 10 & 16 &  6 & 15 & 24 \\
          3 &  6 &  6 &  9 & 12 & 18 &  9 & 18 & 27 \\
          8 & 10 & 20 & 32 & 25 & 40 & 12 & 30 & 48 \\
         12 & 15 & 24 & 36 & 30 & 45 & 18 & 36 & 54 \\
         \hline
          7 &  8 & 28 & 49 & 32 & 56 &  9 & 36 & 63 \\
         \hline
         14 & 16 & 35 & 56 & 40 & 64 & 18 & 45 & 72 \\
         21 & 24 & 42 & 63 & 48 & 72 & 27 & 54 & 81
       \end{array}\right].
\end{align}</math>

=== Khatri–Rao product ===
{{main|Khatri–Rao product}}
* Block Kronecker product
* Column-wise Khatri–Rao product

=== Face-splitting product ===
{{main|Khatri–Rao product}}
Mixed-products properties<ref name="slyusar">
{{cite journal|last=Slyusar|first=V.I.|year=1998|orig-date=27 December 1996|title=End products in matrices in radar applications|url=http://slyusar.kiev.ua/en/IZV_1998_3.pdf|journal=[[Radioelectronics and Communications Systems]]|volume=41|issue=3|pages=50–53}}
</ref>
: <math>\mathbf{A} \otimes (\mathbf{B}\bull \mathbf{C}) = (\mathbf{A}\otimes \mathbf{B}) \bull \mathbf{C} ,</math>

where <math>\bull</math> denotes the [[Khatri–Rao product#Face-splitting product|Face-splitting product]].<ref name="lecture">
{{cite web|last=Slyusar|first=Vadym|year=1999|title=New matrix operations for DSP|url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/342918804|type=self-published lecture|via=[[ResearchGate]]|doi=10.13140/RG.2.2.31620.76164/1}}
</ref><ref name="slyusar2">
{{Cite journal|last=Slyusar|first=V.I.|date=March 13, 1998|title=A Family of Face Products of Matrices and its Properties|url=http://slyusar.kiev.ua/FACE.pdf|journal=Cybernetics and Systems Analysis C/C of Kibernetika I Sistemnyi Analiz. 1999|volume=35|issue=3|pages=379–384|doi=10.1007/BF02733426|s2cid=119661450}}
</ref>

: <math>(\mathbf{A} \bull \mathbf{B})(\mathbf{C} \otimes \mathbf{D}) = (\mathbf{A}\mathbf{C}) \bull (\mathbf{B} \mathbf{D}) ,</math>

Similarly:<ref name="DIPED">
{{cite conference|last=Slyusar|first=V.I.|date=1997-09-15|title=New operations of matrices product for applications of radars|url=http://slyusar.kiev.ua/DIPED_1997.pdf|conference=Direct and Inverse Problems of Electromagnetic and Acoustic Wave Theory (DIPED-97), Lviv.|pages=73–74}}
</ref>
: <math>(\mathbf{A} \bull \mathbf{L})(\mathbf{B} \otimes \mathbf{M}) \cdots (\mathbf{C} \otimes \mathbf{S}) = (\mathbf{A}\mathbf{B} \cdots \mathbf{C}) \bull (\mathbf{L}\mathbf{M} \cdots \mathbf{S}) ,</math>

: <math>\mathbf{c}^\textsf{T} \bull \mathbf{d}^\textsf{T} = \mathbf{c}^\textsf{T} \otimes \mathbf{d}^\textsf{T} , </math>

where <math>\mathbf c</math> and <math>\mathbf d</math> are [[vector (mathematics and physics)|vector]]s,<ref name="tensorsketch">
{{cite arXiv|eprint=1909.01821|first1=Thomas Dybdahl|last1=Ahle|first2=Jakob Bæk Tejs|last2=Knudsen|title=Almost optimal tensor sketch|date=2019-09-03|class=cs.DS}}
</ref>

: <math>(\mathbf{A} \bull \mathbf{B})(\mathbf{c} \otimes \mathbf{d}) = (\mathbf{A}\mathbf{c}) \circ (\mathbf{B}\mathbf{d}) ,</math>

where <math>\mathbf c</math> and <math>\mathbf d</math> are [[vector (mathematics and physics)|vector]]s, and <math>\circ</math> denotes the [[Hadamard product (matrices)|Hadamard product]].

Similarly:
: <math>(\mathbf{A} \bull \mathbf{B})(\mathbf{M}\mathbf{N}\mathbf{c} \otimes \mathbf{Q}\mathbf{P}\mathbf{d}) = (\mathbf{A}\mathbf{M}\mathbf{N}\mathbf{c}) \circ (\mathbf{B}\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{P}\mathbf{d}),</math>
: <math>\mathcal F(C^{(1)}x \star C^{(2)}y) = (\mathcal F C^{(1)} \bull \mathcal F C^{(2)})(x \otimes y)= \mathcal F C^{(1)}x \circ \mathcal F C^{(2)}y,  </math>

where <math>\star</math> is vector [[convolution]] and <math>\mathcal F</math> is the [[DFT matrix|Fourier transform matrix]] (this result is an evolving of [[count sketch]] properties<ref name="ninh">
{{cite conference 
 | last1 = Ninh   | first1 = Pham
 | first2 = Rasmus | last2 = Pagh | author2-link = Rasmus Pagh
 | date = 2013
 | title = Fast and scalable polynomial kernels via explicit feature maps
 | conference = SIGKDD international conference on Knowledge discovery and data mining
 | publisher = Association for Computing Machinery
 | doi = 10.1145/2487575.2487591
}}
</ref>),<ref name="lecture" /><ref name="slyusar2" />

: <math>(\mathbf{A} \bull \mathbf{L})(\mathbf{B} \otimes \mathbf{M}) \cdots (\mathbf{C} \otimes \mathbf{S})(\mathbf{K} \ast \mathbf{T}) = (\mathbf{A}\mathbf{B} \cdot \mathbf{C}\mathbf{K}) \circ (\mathbf{L}\mathbf{M} \cdots \mathbf{S}\mathbf{T}) ,</math>

where <math>\ast</math> denotes the [[Khatri–Rao product#Column-wise Khatri–Rao product|column-wise Khatri–Rao product]].

Similarly:
: <math>(\mathbf{A} \bull \mathbf{L})(\mathbf{B} \otimes \mathbf{M}) \cdots (\mathbf{C} \otimes \mathbf{S})(c \otimes d ) = (\mathbf{A}\mathbf{B} \cdots \mathbf{C}\mathbf{c}) \circ (\mathbf{L}\mathbf{M} \cdots \mathbf{S}\mathbf{d}) ,</math>
: <math>(\mathbf{A} \bull \mathbf{L})(\mathbf{B} \otimes \mathbf{M}) \cdots (\mathbf{C} \otimes \mathbf{S})(\mathbf{P}\mathbf{c} \otimes \mathbf{Q}\mathbf{d} ) = (\mathbf{A}\mathbf{B} \cdots \mathbf{C}\mathbf{P}\mathbf{c}) \circ (\mathbf{L}\mathbf{M} \cdots \mathbf{S}\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{d}) ,</math>
where <math>\mathbf c</math> and <math>\mathbf d</math> are [[Vector (mathematics and physics)|vector]]s.
